newsitem.title: INDIA: India says population outstripping food growth.
newsitem.headline: India says population outstripping food growth.

text.p: India on Tuesday said it was worried that foodgrains production was not keeping pace with population growth.

"The annual compound growth of foodgrains for the past six years between 1990/91 to 1996/97 at 1.7 percent is lower than the annual population growth of 1.9 percent for the nineties, and, therefore, a matter of serious concern," the government's annual Economic Survey for 1996/97 said.
The government said earlier in February that the country's population was projected to grow to 936 million in 1996/97 (April-March) from 920 million at the end of the previous year.
India, predominantly an agricultural country, had its ninth good monsoon in a row in 1996.
The survey, presented to parliament by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, said even a marginal three to four percent fall in foodgrains output could sharply push up the prices of primary commodities.
It said such a situation had forced the government to draw on foodgrains reserves and go for imports in 1993 and 1996.
As of January 1, 1997, the government held wheat and rice stocks of 19.8 million tonnes compared with 28.5 million a year earlier.
Concerns about foodgrains stocks compelled the government in December to order two million tonnes of wheat imports to augment supplies and check rising prices.
That was a sharp turnaround from the 1995/96 year, when India exported wheat for the first time since Independence from British rule in 1947.
It exported 600,000 tonnes of wheat in 1995/96 and 1.07 million tonnes up to September 30, 1996, when exports ended.
The economic survey projected foodgrains production in 1996/97 (July/June) at 191.2 million tonnes, up from 185 million in the previous year.
Agriculture contributes 29.4 percent of India's GDP, employing 64 percent of the country's workforce.
During the eighth plan (1992/97), agriculture annually grew by 3.5 percent and foodgrains output growth was three percent.
In the ninth plan, beginning April 1, 1997, the government is aiming at a 4.5 percent agriculture growth.

The survey forecast agriculture will grow by 3.0 percent in 1996/97, against a 0.4 percent drop in 1995/96. Foodgrains output in 1996/97 is forecast to grow by 3.3 percent, against a fall of 3.4 percent in the previous year.

The survey said the government must address major brakes on growth including a fall in investment in agriculture, a lack of new seed varieties and restrictions on storage and movement of farm commodities.
"Industrial policy reforms cannot just be treated in isolation with the agricultural sector continuing to remain fettered," the survey said.
It said industry had greatly gained from deregulation, as part of economic reforms launched in 1991, and similar benefits should flow to help agricultural growth.
